stem: Which part of a business proposal sums up the whole plan on one page?

options.content: The executive summary
The risk analysis
options.rationale: The risk analysis lists what could go wrong.

options.content: The staffing plan
options.rationale: The staffing plan says who does what.

options.content: The start-up cost table
options.rationale: The table is only part of the finance section.

explanation: The executive summary is a short version of the whole proposal.

stem: What is the purpose of the market section of a business proposal?

options.content: To show who the customers are, how many there are and who competes for them
To list the staff and their pay
To give the monthly profit
options.rationale: That is part of the finance section.

options.content: To describe how the equipment is repaired and how the spare parts are ordered

explanation: The market section shows that customers exist.

stem: What does the payback period measure?

options.content: The time that a customer takes to pay an invoice after receiving all of the goods ordered
The total revenue in a year
The time it takes for profits to repay the money invested to start the business
The time to repair a device
options.rationale: That is not a financial measure.

explanation: Payback period = start-up cost ÷ profit per period.

stem: Which of these is a start-up cost for a computer repair shop?

options.content: Paying monthly rent
Paying an assistant each month for their work
Buying test equipment before opening
options.rationale: Correct: it is a one-off cost before opening.

options.content: Buying electricity each month

explanation: Start-up costs are spent once, at the beginning.

stem: A proposal states the expected monthly revenue but no costs. Why is this a weakness?

options.content: Revenue is never important
options.rationale: Revenue matters but is not the whole story.

options.content: Revenue alone does not show whether the business makes a profit
Costs are decided by the bank
Customers do not pay for services, so costs are not important to a business

explanation: Profit = revenue − costs.
hints: What is left after costs are paid?

stem: A repair shop plans for 70 jobs a month but a cautious owner also calculates the profit for 50 jobs. What is she doing?

options.content: Writing the executive summary of the plan later
options.rationale: The summary is a short description of the whole plan.

options.content: Testing the plan by changing an assumption
options.rationale: Correct: this shows how sensitive the plan is.

options.content: Choosing a brand name
Registering the business

explanation: Changing an assumption tests viability.
hints: What happens to profit if the customers are fewer?

stem: How is the return on investment (ROI) calculated?

options.content: Annual revenue ÷ amount invested × 100
Amount invested ÷ annual profit
options.rationale: That gives years, similar to payback.

options.content: Monthly costs × 12
options.rationale: That is the annual cost, not ROI.

options.content: Annual profit ÷ amount invested × 100

explanation: ROI is a percentage of the investment.

stem: A bank is asked to lend money for two shops. Shop A pays back in 8 months but depends on one customer. Shop B pays back in 14 months with many customers. Which statement is the best judgement?

options.content: Shop A is always better because 8 is less than 14
options.rationale: Speed of payback ignores the risk.

options.content: Neither can be judged, because banks do not use payback to decide whether to lend money
options.rationale: Payback is one of the measures used.

options.content: Shop B is worse because many customers cause problems
Shop B may be less risky even though it repays more slowly, because it does not depend on one customer

explanation: Viability depends on risk as well as payback.
hints: What happens if the one customer leaves?

stem: The executive summary is usually written last, so that it matches the finished proposal.
explanation: True. It summarises the other sections, so it is written after them.

stem: Match each section of a business proposal to its content.

right.content: Who does what and what skills are needed
Start-up costs, budget, profit and payback
What could go wrong and how it will be reduced
The need that exists for the product or service
Where and how the work is done

explanation: Each section has a distinct purpose.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Money spent once before opening is a {{blank:a}} cost. Revenue minus costs is {{blank:b}}. The time for profit to repay the start-up cost is the {{blank:c}} period.

explanation: Start-up, profit, payback.
hints: Think about money spent once and the money kept each month.

stem: Name the figure calculated as annual profit divided by the amount invested, multiplied by 100.
explanation: Return on investment (ROI).

stem: A web design business buys a computer for US\$640, software licences for US\$210, a desk for US\$180, registration for US\$120 and launch advertising for US\$90. Calculate the total start-up cost, in US dollars.
explanation: The total is 1240.

stem: The shop expects to copy 2600 pages a month at US\$0.10 a page and to do 40 printing jobs at US\$4 each. Its monthly costs are rent US\$90, electricity US\$45 and paper and toner US\$120. Calculate the monthly profit, in US dollars.
hints: Revenue from copies plus revenue from printing jobs, minus the monthly costs.

stem: The start-up cost is US\$2420 and the monthly profit is US\$165. Calculate the payback period in months, to 1 decimal place.
hints: Payback = start-up cost ÷ monthly profit; give the answer to one decimal place.

stem: State four sections of a business proposal and say what each contains. [4]

points.description: Executive summary: a one-page summary of the proposal
Problem and solution: the need and how the business meets it
Market: who the customers and competitors are
Finance: start-up costs, budget, profit and payback (or risks, or staffing)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The executive summary is a one-page summary. The problem and solution describe the need and how the business meets it. The market shows who the customers and competitors are. The finance section gives start-up costs, budget, profit and payback.

explanation: Any four sections described.
hints: Name four sections and say what each contains.

stem: Describe an ICT business that could be started in a rural town in Zimbabwe, stating the problem it solves and its customers. [4]

points.description: A named ICT business, for example a phone charging and repair shop or a computer training centre
A real problem it solves, for example few places to charge or repair phones
The customers: for example families, learners and small traders
How it earns money, for example a fee for each charge, repair or course

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A phone charging and repair shop in a rural town. It solves the problem that there are few places to charge or repair phones. Its customers are families, learners and small traders, and it earns a fee for each charge or repair.

explanation: Business, problem, customers and income.
hints: Think about the problem, solution, customers and staff.

stem: State three risks to a new computer repair shop and one way to reduce each. [3]

points.description: Fewer customers than expected: advertise at schools and offer a guarantee
Theft or damage of stock: lock the stock, insure it or keep a stock record
Power cuts: use a surge protector or small uninterruptible power supply

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Fewer customers than expected: advertise at schools and offer a guarantee. Theft of stock: keep it locked and insured. Power cuts: use a surge protector or small uninterruptible power supply.

explanation: Any three risks with a way to reduce each.
hints: Think about threats to income and to stock.

stem: A bank is considering lending US\$3000 to start a shop that would make a profit of US\$125 a month. Evaluate whether the shop looks viable. [4]

points.description: The payback period is 3000 ÷ 125 = 24 months, which is two years
The annual profit is 125 × 12 = US\$1500, so the return on investment is 1500 ÷ 3000 × 100 = 50%
A long payback is risky if customers or prices change, so the plan should be tested with fewer customers
A judgement, for example that it is viable if the forecast is realistic and the risks are controlled, or that the bank should ask for more evidence

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The payback period is 3000 ÷ 125 = 24 months and the ROI is 1500 ÷ 3000 × 100 = 50%. A two-year payback is risky if customers or prices change, so the plan should be tested with fewer customers. It looks viable only if the forecast is realistic and the risks are controlled.

explanation: Calculate, comment on risk, judge.
hints: Compare the payback period and ROI with risk.

stem:
A graduate in Masvingo plans a printing and photocopying shop.

Start-up costs:

| Start-up cost | Amount (US\$) |
|:-:|:-:|
| Photocopier | 1350 |
| Computer and printer | 520 |
| Furniture | 280 |
| Licence and registration | 140 |
| Launch advertising | 130 |

Each month she expects revenue of US\$420 and costs of rent US\$90, electricity US\$45 and paper and toner US\$120.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the total start-up cost, in US dollars.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the monthly profit, in US dollars.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the return on investment, as a percentage to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State two pieces of advice the graduate should be given before she starts the business.

points.description: Test the plan with fewer customers than expected to see if it is still profitable
Do market research to confirm that enough customers will use the shop, or write a plan for risks such as theft and power cuts

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Test the plan with fewer customers than expected, and do market research to confirm that enough customers will use the shop.

explanation: Start-up US\$2420; monthly profit US\$165; payback 14.7 months; ROI 82%.
hints: Total costs = rent + electricity + paper and toner.

stem: A computer training centre in Bulawayo needs US\$1800 to start and expects a profit of US\$150 a month.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the payback period in months.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the return on investment as a percentage.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Give two risks to the training centre and a way to reduce each.

points.description: Few learners enrol: advertise at schools and offer a trial class
Power cuts stop lessons: use a surge protector or small uninterruptible power supply, or a generator or solar power

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Few learners enrol: advertise at schools and offer a trial class. Power cuts stop lessons: use a surge protector or small uninterruptible power supply, or solar power.

explanation: The training centre repays in 12 months with an ROI of 100%.
hints: Payback = start-up cost ÷ monthly profit; ROI = annual profit ÷ investment × 100.

stem: Chipo wants to start a business that supplies attendance and fees software to primary schools in Masvingo.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the problem that her business solves and the solution she offers.

points.description: Problem: schools record attendance and fees on paper, which is slow and has errors
Solution: simple software that records and reports them on one computer

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Schools record attendance and fees on paper, which is slow and has errors. Her software records and reports them on one computer.

points.description: Primary schools with at least one computer, and head teachers or bursars who decide to buy
Competitors: other software suppliers or schools that keep using paper; reached through the district office and demonstrations

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Primary schools with at least one computer, where head teachers or bursars decide to buy. Competitors are other suppliers or schools that keep using paper, and she can reach schools through the district office and demonstrations.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State two items of start-up cost for her business.

points.description: A computer and equipment for development and demonstrations
Registration and licences, or launch advertising, or travel to schools

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A computer and equipment for development and demonstrations, and registration, licences and launch advertising.

explanation: Each section is applied to a school software supplier.
hints: Each section should be linked to the school software business.
